en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question on Inference.
2. The Question on Ascetic Practices “Venerable Nāgasena, do all Bodhisattvas perform ascetic practices, or was it only the Bodhisattva Gotama who performed ascetic practices?
“There is no performance of ascetic practices by all Bodhisattvas, Great King; it was only by the Bodhisattva Gotama that ascetic practices were performed.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, if this is so, it is improper that there should be a difference among Bodhisattvas.
“There are four grounds, Great King, on which there is a difference among Bodhisattvas. Which four? [The Teacher then enumerates them.]”
"Difference in family, difference in exertion, difference in lifespan, and difference in physical stature.
It is through these four points, Great King, that there is a distinction among Bodhisattvas.
However, Great King, for all Buddhas, there is no distinction in form, virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation."

“In the four grounds of self-confidence, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the six unique knowledges, the fourteen Buddha-knowledges, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, and in all the qualities of a Buddha, there is no diversity; all Buddhas are exactly equal in their Buddha-qualities.
“If, venerable Nāgasena, all Buddhas are exactly equal in their Buddha-qualities, for what reason was the practice of austerities performed only by the Bodhisatta Gotama?”

“Great King, while his knowledge was still unripened and his enlightenment unripened, the Bodhisatta Gotama went forth into homelessness; he performed austerities in order to ripen that unripened knowledge.

“Venerable Nāgasena, for what reason did the Bodhisatta go forth on the Great Renunciation while his knowledge was still unripened and his enlightenment unripened? Should one not rather have gone forth after having ripened the knowledge, once the knowledge was ripe?”
“Great King, when the Bodhisatta saw the women’s quarters in their perverse state, he became remorseful;

in that one who was remorseful, a sense of aversion arose. Seeing that a mind of aversion had arisen, a certain son of the gods belonging to Māra’s host, standing in the air, thinking, ‘This is indeed the time to dispel the mind of aversion,’ spoke these words:”

“Friend, do not be despondent. On the seventh day from now, a divine wheel-treasure will appear to you—thousand-spoked, with a rim and a hub, complete in every respect—and the treasures both on the earth and in the sky will come to you of their own accord.
Among the two thousand minor islands that surround [this world],”
"Your command shall prevail with one voice over the four great continents;
you shall have more than a thousand sons, brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies; surrounded by those sons, endowed with the seven treasures, you shall rule over the four continents."
"Just as, Great King, an iron spike heated all day long, burning everywhere, might enter the ear canal—even so, Great King, did those words of the deity enter the Bodhisatta’s ear.
Thus, already dissatisfied by nature, he became even more terrified, agitated, and filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) by that deity’s words.
And just as, Great King, a great mass of blazing fire, when fanned by another piece of wood, would burn even more intensely."

In the same way, Great King, the Bodhisatta was already weary by nature, but by the words of that deity he became even more agitated, alarmed, and filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

Or just as, Great King, the great earth, naturally parched yet having produced green grass and foliage, becomes even more muddy when water is poured upon it after a great rain cloud has fallen; so it was with him.

“In the very same way, Great King, the Bodhisatta was already weary by his own nature, but by the words of that deity he became even more agitated, alarmed, and filled with a sense of spiritual urgency.
“But, venerable Nāgasena, if the divine Wheel-Treasure were to appear for the Bodhisatta on the seventh day, would the Bodhisatta turn back once the divine Wheel-Treasure had appeared?
“Certainly not, Great King; the divine Wheel-Treasure would not appear for the Bodhisatta on the seventh day.”
And what that deity spoke was a falsehood intended for seduction; even if, O Great King, the divine Wheel-Treasure were to appear on the seventh day, the Bodhisatta would not turn back.
What is the reason?
“‘It is impermanent,’ Great King, the Bodhisatta grasped firmly; ‘it is suffering’ and ‘it is non-self,’ he grasped firmly, and thus he attained the destruction of clinging.

Just as, Great King, water from Lake Anotatta enters the river Gaṅgā, the river Gaṅgā enters the great ocean, and from the great ocean it enters the mouth of Pātāla—would that water, Great King, having reached the mouth of Pātāla, [ever return]?”
“Suppose it were to turn back and enter the great ocean; from the great ocean it were to enter the river Gaṅgā;
and from the river Gaṅgā it were to enter Anotatta again.
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“In the same way, Great King, for the sake of this final existence, the Bodhisatta has cultivated wholesome merit for four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons.
This is his last birth; having reached full maturity in the knowledge of enlightenment, he will become a Buddha in six years—the Omniscient One, the Supreme Person in the world. Would it not be so?”
“Great King, would the Bodhisatta turn back for the sake of the Wheel-Treasure?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“Furthermore, Great King, even if the great earth with its forests and mountains were to turn upside down, the Bodhisatta would never turn back until he has attained supreme perfect enlightenment.”
Even if, Great King, the waters of the Ganges were to flow back upstream, the Bodhisatta would not turn back until he had attained supreme enlightenment;
even if, Great King, the great ocean, with its immeasurable waters, were to dry up like the water in a cow’s footprint, the Bodhisatta would not turn back until he had attained supreme enlightenment;
even if, Great King, Sineru, the king of mountains, were to split into a hundred or a thousand pieces, the Bodhisatta would not turn back until he had attained supreme enlightenment.
"Even if, O Great King, the moon and sun together with the stars were to fall to the ground like a clod of earth, the Bodhisatta would not turn back until he had attained full enlightenment.
Even if, O Great King, space were to contract like a mat, the Bodhisatta would not turn back until he had attained full enlightenment.
For what reason?"
“Because all bonds have been torn asunder.
“Venerable Nāgasena, how many bonds are there in the world?
“There are, O Great King, these ten bonds in the world, by which bonds bound beings do not escape; and even having escaped, they return again.”
Which ten?
Great King, a mother is a bond in the world; great King, a father is a bond in the world; great King, a wife is a bond in the world;
great King, children are a bond in the world; great King, kinsmen are a bond in the world.
Friendship, Great King, is a bond in the world; wealth, Great King, is a bond in the world; gain and honor, Great King, are bonds in the world;
sovereignty, Great King, is a bond in the world; the five strands of sensual pleasure, Great King, are bonds in the world.
These, Great King, are the ten bonds in the world, by which beings are bound.
“Beings do not depart [from the cycle], and even having departed, they return; those ten fetters have been cut and shattered by the Bodhisatta.
Therefore, Great King, the Bodhisatta does not turn back.
“Venerable Nāgasena, if the Bodhisatta, when a mind of aversion had arisen and while his faculties were still unripened, [did not turn back] because of the words of a deity...”
“Since he has gone forth into renunciation while his knowledge regarding enlightenment was still unripened, what is the use of his performing such difficult austerities?
Should he not rather have been an eater of all things, waiting for the ripening of his knowledge?
“But, Great King, there are these ten types of persons in the world who are despised, looked down upon, reviled, mocked, censured, treated with contempt, and held in low esteem.”
Which ten?
A woman who is a widow, Great King, is despised, looked down upon, reviled, ridiculed, censured, treated with contempt, and disregarded in the world.
A person who is weak, Great King... [and so forth].
A person who is a friend of enemies, great king;
a person who eats excessively, great king;
a person who dwells in the homes of others, great king.
A person with evil friends, great king, is such a person;
a person devoid of wealth, great king, is such a person;
a person devoid of proper conduct, great king, is such a person.
"A person devoid of action, great king, and a person devoid of effort,
great king, are despised, held in contempt, reviled, mocked, censured, treated with disregard, and not respected in the world. These, great king,
are the ten persons who are despised, held in contempt, reviled, mocked, censured, treated with disregard, and not respected in the world."
"Great King, as the Bodhisatta was recollecting these ten points, this perception arose in him:
'May I not be deficient in action, deficient in effort, or censured by gods and humans;
what if I were to be one who acts, who values action, who is dominated by action, whose nature is action, who is devoted to action, who dwells in the abode of action, and who lives with diligence?'"
“In this way, Great King, the Bodhisatta, while maturing his knowledge, performed difficult austerities.
“Venerable Nāgasena, when the Bodhisatta was performing difficult austerities, he said:
‘Indeed, by means of these bitter austerities, I do not attain any superhuman state, nor any distinction in noble knowledge and vision that is worthy of the Ariyans.’”
"Could there perhaps be another path to enlightenment?
At that time, was there any lapse in the Bodhisatta’s mindfulness regarding the path?
"Great King, there are these twenty-five things that weaken the mind; when the mind is weakened by them, it does not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints."
Which twenty-five?

Anger, Great King, is a state that weakens the mind; by it, the weakened mind does not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. Resentment... [and so on] ...slander... [and so on] ...
... envy ...
jealousy ...
stinginess ...
Deceit … guile … obstinacy …
Aggression … conceit … overweening pride …
Intoxication … negligence … sloth and torpor …
Laziness … indolence … association with evil friends …
Forms … sounds … odors …
Tastes … tangible objects … hunger and thirst …
“Discontent, Great King, is a state that weakens the mind; when the mind is weakened by it, it does not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
These, Great King, are the twenty-five states that weaken the mind, by which a weakened mind does not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
Furthermore, Great King, hunger and thirst consumed the Bodhisatta’s body; when his body was consumed, his mind did not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.”
"Great King, for one hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable aeons,

the Bodhisatta sought the realization of the Four Noble Truths throughout those various births; how then could there be any lapse of mindfulness regarding the Path in his final birth, the birth of realization?"
Moreover, Great King, a mere perception arose in the Bodhisatta: ‘Could there perhaps be another path to enlightenment?

Previously, Great King, when the Bodhisatta was one month old, while his father Suddhodana was at work, he sat cross-legged upon a splendid couch in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states.
“Having attained and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and happiness...
[and so on] ...he attained and dwelt in the fourth jhāna.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as such: while maturing his wisdom, the Bodhisatta performed the practice of austerities.”
The second question: On Difficult Deeds.
